row.basis: The word near at mouth and heart
row.note: The commentary says the feminine “it” is the reminder offered in 87:9 and that the worst person keeps it beside him yet at a remove; Deuteronomy says the command is not far away but very near, in mouth and heart, to be done.

row.basis: “Depart from us” and rejected knowledge
row.note: The commentary makes the ashqa actively turn away from the reminder; Job quotes the wicked saying to God to depart and that they do not desire knowledge of his ways, a direct speech of refusal, while Job’s context complicates any claim that such rejection is always punished immediately.

row.basis: Wisdom calls and is refused
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder is offered and the difference begins in the hearer; Wisdom says she called and was refused, making rejection rather than the offer the decisive act.

row.basis: Counsel and reproof rejected
row.note: The commentary’s “most wretched” turns aside from admonition; Wisdom says her counsel was rejected and her reproof ignored, then describes the consequence of that response.

row.basis: Turning the ear from Torah
row.note: The commentary treats turning from reminder as choosing wrongly what to keep at one’s side; Proverbs says the person who turns an ear away from hearing Torah makes even prayer abhorrent.

row.basis: Not listening and walking backward
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the unchanged reminder from the hearer’s response; Jeremiah says the people did not listen or incline their ear, but followed their own counsel and went backward.

row.basis: Stopping the ear against prophetic words
row.note: The commentary’s ashqa keeps the reminder at hand but declines it; Zechariah says the people refused to hear, turned a stubborn shoulder, and stopped their ears against the law and the words sent through prophets.

row.basis: A hardened heart and unanswered warning
row.note: The commentary connects rejection of the reminder with the person’s own chosen posture; Zechariah says they made their hearts hard so they would not hear the law or prophetic words, followed by the Lord’s anger.

row.basis: Hearing without doing
row.note: The commentary says the reminder itself is unchanged while people respond differently; Ezekiel’s hearers come, sit before the prophet, and hear his words, but do not do them because their hearts pursue gain.

row.basis: The prophet as a pleasing song
row.note: The commentary’s image of keeping admonition nearby yet treating it as alien fits Ezekiel’s hearers, who enjoy the prophet’s voice like a lovely song while not carrying out what he says.

row.basis: “Today” as an open moment to hear
row.note: The commentary presents one reminder offered to all, with the response still open; the psalm addresses its hearers as God’s people and says that today they hear his voice.

row.basis: Do not harden the heart
row.note: The commentary contrasts the one who takes warning with the one who avoids it; the psalm warns its hearers not to harden their hearts as in the wilderness rebellion.

row.basis: The Rechabites obey while Judah will not hear
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder reaches different hearers; Jeremiah contrasts Rechabites who kept their father’s command with Judah, which did not listen when God spoke persistently through prophets.

row.basis: A messenger must speak whether hearers heed or refuse
row.note: The commentary separates the act of offering reminder from its reception; Ezekiel is told that the rebellious may hear or refuse, but will know a prophet has been among them.

row.basis: Responsibility after a warning is given
row.note: The commentary says the messenger offers admonition without controlling the hearer; Ezekiel’s watchman is delivered from guilt after warning, while the warned wicked person remains accountable if he does not turn.

row.basis: Repeated messengers sent in compassion
row.note: The commentary emphasizes a single shared call and differing reception; Chronicles says God repeatedly sent messengers because he had compassion on his people and dwelling place.

row.basis: Mocking and despising the words
row.note: The commentary’s worst person avoids the reminder and faces its consequence; Chronicles says the people mocked God’s messengers, despised his words, and scoffed at the prophets until judgment came.

row.basis: Rejecting knowledge and forgetting Torah
row.note: The commentary links the wretched condition to turning away from reminder; Hosea names the people’s rejection of knowledge and forgetting of God’s law as the cause of their ruin.

row.basis: Nineveh receives the warning
row.note: The commentary says the offered reminder is the same while its hearers divide by response; in Jonah, the people of Nineveh believe the warning and undertake repentance rather than dismiss it.

row.basis: Turning from evil changes the outcome
row.note: The commentary contrasts turning away from reminder with self-correction; Jonah says God saw that Nineveh turned from its evil way and relented from the announced disaster.

row.basis: Human choice and self-directed action
row.note: The commentary reads the response verbs as acts a person does upon oneself; Sirach says God left human beings in the hand of their own inclination, giving a Jewish wisdom parallel for accountable response.

row.basis: Fire and water set before the hearer
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder is offered but people choose their response; Sirach pictures fire and water before the person, who stretches out a hand to whichever he chooses.

row.basis: Life and death as alternatives
row.note: The commentary places the wretched person at the far end of a chosen response; Sirach explicitly sets life and death before human beings and says each receives what he chooses.

row.basis: Abraham’s family served other gods
row.note: The commentary recalls Abraham asking God to keep him and his sons from idol worship; Joshua says Abraham’s ancestors, including Terah, served other gods, supplying the biblical background to the Qur’anic break with idolatry.

row.basis: The word received and made fruitful
row.note: The commentary contrasts one who takes reminder with the one who avoids it; Mark’s good soil hears the word, accepts it, and bears fruit, a concrete positive reception.

row.basis: Hearing and doing as the wise response
row.note: The commentary reads taking reminder and purifying oneself as actions a person undertakes; Jesus calls the hearer who does his words wise and compares him to a house built on rock.

row.basis: Hearing without doing as the ruinous response
row.note: The commentary’s ashqa hears the reminder’s availability yet turns aside; Jesus describes the hearer who does not do his words, whose house falls when the same storm comes.

row.basis: Moses and the Prophets are already available
row.note: The commentary says the reminder has been delivered and the hearer is responsible for receiving it; Abraham in the parable tells the rich man’s brothers that they have Moses and the Prophets to hear.

row.basis: A further sign will not cure refusal to hear
row.note: The commentary says those avoiding reminder cannot blame its absence; the parable answers that those who do not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.

row.basis: Felix fears, then sends Paul away
row.note: The commentary contrasts the one who fears and receives warning with the worst person who turns from it; as Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control, and coming judgment, Felix becomes afraid and tells him to go away.

row.basis: Resisting the Spirit as the ancestors did
row.note: The commentary portrays turning away from reminder as a repeated response to divine messengers; Stephen accuses his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit and doing as their ancestors did when they rejected the prophets.

row.basis: Turning away from the living God
row.note: The commentary’s verb makes withdrawal the person’s own act; Hebrews warns against an unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.

row.basis: Do not harden the heart when the voice is heard
row.note: The commentary links the reminder to a present chance to respond; Hebrews repeats the psalm’s “Today” warning not to harden the heart upon hearing God’s voice.

row.basis: The message heard but not beneficial
row.note: The commentary says one unchanged reminder benefits one hearer while another avoids it; Hebrews says the good news came to its hearers but did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith.

row.basis: One proclamation among both saved and perishing
row.note: The commentary stresses one reminder offered to all with different reception; Paul calls the apostolic proclamation an aroma of Christ among both those being saved and those perishing.

row.basis: The same word as life or death
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder yields benefit to one and loss to another; Paul describes the proclamation as an aroma from death to death for one group and from life to life for another.

row.basis: The word of the cross divides hearers
row.note: The commentary says the reminder itself is unchanged while people receive it differently; Paul says the word of the cross is foolishness to those perishing and God’s power to those being saved.

row.basis: Doers, not hearers only
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that the person does something to himself by taking or avoiding reminder; James tells hearers to become doers of the word and not deceive themselves by hearing alone.

row.basis: The hearer who sees and forgets
row.note: The commentary contrasts the Prophet’s preserved recitation with the person who lets reminder pass; James likens the hearer who does not act to someone who looks at his face in a mirror.

row.basis: The hearer turns away and forgets
row.note: The commentary’s image is of one who moves the reminder aside; James says the inactive hearer goes away and immediately forgets what he was like.

row.basis: Persevering in the word and doing it
row.note: The commentary links self-directed purification to sustained action; James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the one who looks into the law, perseveres, and acts.

row.basis: One sermon meets mockery and postponement
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is offered but response divides hearers; after Paul speaks of resurrection, some mock and others postpone hearing him again.

row.basis: Some hearers join and believe
row.note: The commentary contrasts the worst person with one who takes the reminder; Acts adds that some listeners join Paul and believe after the same speech that others mocked.

row.basis: Not all obey the good news they hear
row.note: The commentary makes reception rather than delivery the point of division; Paul says not all obeyed the good news and cites the question of who believed the report.

row.basis: Jesus’ words are offered for salvation
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is given for benefit, even though its hearers may turn away; Jesus says he came to save the world rather than judge the one who hears his words.

row.basis: The rejected word judges its hearer
row.note: The commentary connects avoiding reminder with the coming fire and consequence; Jesus says the one who rejects him and does not receive his words has a judge, and the word will judge him on the last day.

row.basis: Seeking death but unable to die
row.note: The commentary reads the condemned state as neither dying nor living; Revelation says those tormented in the vision seek death but cannot find it, a striking parallel with the refusal of death as release.

row.basis: Abraham taken from beyond the River
row.note: The commentary says Abraham asks God to keep him away from idols rather than trusting his own power; Joshua recalls God taking Abraham from beyond the River and leading him, a related account of Abraham’s separation under divine guidance.

row.basis: Pharaoh refuses Moses’ demand
row.note: The commentary describes Moses inviting Pharaoh to purify himself and then Pharaoh denying and turning away; Exodus has Pharaoh answer Moses and Aaron by asking who the Lord is and refusing to obey his voice, a shared confrontation whose wording and demand differ.

row.basis: Two outcomes placed before Israel
row.note: The commentary develops the division between the one who remembers and the one who avoids reminder; Deuteronomy sets life and good against death and evil before Israel as a covenant decision.

row.basis: “Choose life” after the warning
row.note: The commentary says the response, not the offered reminder, divides people; Moses calls heaven and earth to witness and urges Israel to choose life, making the decision explicit.

row.basis: Wisdom speaks publicly in the streets
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is not delivered privately to only one favored hearer; Proverbs portrays Wisdom crying aloud in public places, where the invitation can be heard before some reject it.

row.basis: Eating the fruit of one’s own way
row.note: The commentary describes the response as what a person does to himself by moving the reminder aside; Wisdom says the refusers will eat the fruit of their own way, making consequence follow chosen conduct.

row.basis: Safety for the one who listens
row.note: The commentary contrasts the ashqa with the one who takes reminder; Wisdom promises that the one who listens will dwell securely, giving the positive outcome beside the warning of refusal.

row.basis: A people unwilling to hear instruction
row.note: The commentary describes people who choose to turn from reminder; Isaiah calls the people rebellious children unwilling to hear the Lord’s instruction.

row.basis: Requesting smooth words instead of warning
row.note: The commentary says the wretched person treats beneficial reminder as something to avoid; Isaiah’s hearers tell seers not to see and ask for smooth, agreeable things rather than truth.

row.basis: Prophets sent repeatedly, but no listening
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the universal offer from the hearer’s response; Jeremiah says the Lord persistently sent prophets, yet the people did not listen or incline their ear.

row.basis: A call to turn from evil is ignored
row.note: The commentary links rejecting reminder with refusing the offered chance to change; Jeremiah recounts repeated calls to turn from evil and serve God, which Judah did not heed.

row.basis: Neighbors invite one another to hear the prophet
row.note: The commentary’s side image says the reminder is beside the person, not far away; Ezekiel describes people speaking to one another and inviting one another to hear the Lord’s word from the prophet.

row.basis: Seek the Lord while near
row.note: The commentary says the rejected reminder has reached the hearer and remains within reach; Isaiah urges seeking the Lord while he may be found and calling while he is near.

row.basis: Turning back is still invited
row.note: The commentary contrasts the person who takes the reminder with the person who avoids it; Isaiah calls the wicked to forsake his way and return to the Lord for mercy.

row.basis: The resident alien is to be loved as oneself
row.note: The commentary develops “foreign neighbor” as an image for someone kept beside but treated as unrelated; Leviticus commands Israel to love the resident alien as oneself, an ethical counterpoint to treating the nearby reminder as foreign.

row.basis: A famine of hearing the Lord’s words
row.note: The commentary stresses that the reminder is offered now and can be put aside; Amos announces a later famine of hearing the Lord’s words, a reversal in which people will lack what the commentary’s hearers still have.

row.basis: Searching for a word that cannot be found
row.note: The commentary says the wretched person lets a present reminder pass by; Amos portrays people wandering in search of the Lord’s word and not finding it, sharpening the cost of refusing it while available.

row.basis: Unquenched fire and undying worm
row.note: The commentary connects the worst person’s refusal with the great fire and the condition of neither dying nor living; Isaiah pictures the corpses of rebels under an unquenched fire and undying worm, sharing persistent judgment imagery but describing corpses rather than the same paradox of living punishment.

row.basis: The wicked later see the righteous vindicated
row.note: The commentary says the one who avoids reminder discovers too late what he has lost; Wisdom depicts the wicked seeing the righteous honored and confessing that they once misjudged him.

row.basis: A belated confession of straying from truth
row.note: The commentary connects refusal of reminder to a path whose loss becomes clear after judgment; Wisdom’s wicked confess that they strayed from the way of truth and did not know the path of righteousness.

row.basis: Two spirits and two paths to opposed outcomes
row.note: The commentary develops a person’s response as the dividing choice between outcomes; the Community Rule organizes human conduct under spirits and paths of truth/light or perversity/darkness, giving a Second Temple Jewish version of moral division.

row.basis: The seed is the word
row.note: The commentary says the one reminder is offered while reception differs; Jesus identifies the seed as the word, so the parable makes the hearer’s response determine whether the same sowing bears fruit.

row.basis: Initial reception can fail under pressure
row.note: The commentary’s “remembering” is not merely hearing once; Mark describes hearers who receive the word with joy but fall away when tribulation or persecution comes.

row.basis: Worldly cares choke the word
row.note: The commentary connects rejection of reminder to preferring worldly life; Mark says cares, wealth’s deceit, and other desires enter and choke the word so it becomes fruitless.

row.basis: Hearing without understanding or turning
row.note: The commentary distinguishes a person who receives reminder from one who turns away; Jesus cites Isaiah about people who hear without understanding and have closed their eyes lest they turn and be healed.

row.basis: Jerusalem was unwilling to be gathered
row.note: The commentary says the reminder can be offered while its audience chooses distance; Jesus laments that he wanted to gather Jerusalem’s children but they were unwilling.

row.basis: Take care how you hear
row.note: The commentary says response to the reminder, not its delivery, distinguishes hearers; Jesus warns listeners to take care how they hear, since what one has can be taken away or increased.

row.basis: The rich man turns away from a life-giving invitation
row.note: The commentary connects avoidance of reminder with preferring worldly life; Mark says the man who was invited to sell his possessions and follow Jesus went away grieving because he had great wealth.

row.basis: Cleanse yourselves and draw near
row.note: The commentary reads purification as work a person does upon himself; James calls double-minded people to cleanse their hands, purify their hearts, and draw near to God.

row.basis: The hopeful person purifies himself
row.note: The commentary groups remembering, avoiding, and purifying as self-directed actions; John says the one who hopes in Christ purifies himself as Christ is pure.

row.basis: The warning remains “Today”
row.note: The commentary treats reminder as presently available and response as decisive; Hebrews says God again appoints a day called Today and repeats the warning not to harden the heart.

row.basis: No rest from the torment
row.note: The commentary’s condemned person neither dies nor lives and endures prolonged hardship; Revelation says the worshippers of the beast have no rest day or night, a related but differently framed image of unending punishment.

row.basis: Welcoming the stranger
row.note: The commentary develops the nearby reminder as treated like a foreign neighbor; Jesus identifies himself with the stranger who is welcomed, making reception of the socially distant one a test of response.

row.basis: The unquenched fire
row.note: The commentary connects the worst person with the great fire and an unending state; Jesus invokes Gehenna where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched, sharing persistence imagery without equating the scenes.

row.basis: Two ways, life and death
row.note: The commentary develops a sharp division between the one who takes reminder and the one who avoids it; the Didache opens by setting out a way of life and a way of death and stressing the great difference between them.

row.basis: The way of death
row.note: The commentary names a worst person by the path he chooses; the Didache’s catalogue of the way of death includes people who hate truth and love falsehood, giving an early Christian moral portrait of that path.

row.basis: Way of light and way of darkness
row.note: The commentary’s paired outcomes turn on a person’s response; Barnabas opens its “Two Ways” teaching with the way of light and the way of darkness, adding an early Christian moral framework for opposed paths.

row.basis: The word accomplishes its purpose
row.note: The commentary emphasizes a reminder whose hearers may take it or turn away; Isaiah says the word sent by God will accomplish what he desires, a different emphasis on the efficacy of the divine word rather than a claim that every hearer responds alike.

row.basis: Fear of the Lord and despising instruction
row.note: The commentary contrasts the one who fears and remembers with the ashqa who avoids reminder; Proverbs makes fear of the Lord the beginning of knowledge and says fools despise wisdom and instruction.

row.basis: Finding Wisdom and finding life
row.note: The commentary sets the one who receives reminder against the one who turns aside; Wisdom says finding her brings life and favor from the Lord.

row.basis: Harming oneself by hating Wisdom
row.note: The commentary says the wretched person makes his own condition by putting the reminder aside; Wisdom says the one who misses her harms himself and those who hate her love death.

row.basis: Despising a word brings ruin
row.note: The commentary links avoiding the offered reminder to the ashqa’s ruin; Proverbs says the person who despises a word will be destroyed, while reverence for the command brings reward.

row.basis: Israel would not hear the Lord
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder is offered but some turn from it; the psalm says God’s people would not listen to his voice or submit to him.

row.basis: Handed over to one’s own counsel
row.note: The commentary treats turning away as the hearer’s own choice; the psalm says God gave the unheeding people over to their stubborn hearts to walk in their own counsels.

row.basis: Willingness and obedience bring good
row.note: The commentary says one person takes the reminder while another rejects it; Isaiah places willingness and obedience opposite rebellion, with the former receiving the land’s good.

row.basis: Refusal and rebellion bring judgment
row.note: The commentary links the ashqa’s avoidance with the consequence of his chosen response; Isaiah says those who refuse and rebel will be devoured by the sword.

row.basis: Called, but not answered
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that the reminder has already come to the hearer; Isaiah says God called and spoke but the people did not answer or hear, instead choosing what displeased him.

row.basis: The offered path is refused
row.note: The commentary contrasts receiving reminder with turning aside; Jeremiah invites the people to stand at the crossroads and ask for the good ancient path, but they answer that they will not walk in it.

row.basis: The watchmen’s warning is not heard
row.note: The commentary separates the messenger’s act of warning from the audience’s response; Jeremiah says watchmen sounded the trumpet, but the people replied that they would not listen.

row.basis: Rejecting the word of the Lord
row.note: The commentary identifies the ashqa by his refusal of reminder; Jeremiah says the wise have rejected the word of the Lord, so their claim to wisdom is exposed.

row.basis: Circumcising the heart
row.note: The commentary reads remembering, avoiding, and purifying as acts done upon oneself; Moses calls Israel to circumcise the heart and stop being stiff-necked, a concrete demand for inward change.

row.basis: Do not postpone good when it is at hand
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is beside the hearer yet treated as a foreign neighbor; Proverbs says not to tell a neighbor to return tomorrow when the needed good is already with you, an ethical parallel to leaving available good within reach unused.

row.basis: Delighting in Torah day and night
row.note: The commentary pictures the reminder as something one may take near and work into oneself; Psalm 1 describes the blessed person delighting in the Lord’s Torah and meditating on it continually.

row.basis: Two ways with opposed endings
row.note: The commentary develops a split between the one who receives reminder and the one who avoids it; Psalm 1 says the Lord knows the righteous way while the wicked way perishes.

row.basis: Rain watering the earth
row.note: The commentary’s lexical aside links the south wind and its clouds with the pasture scene in 87:4; Psalm 65 describes God watering the earth and blessing its growth, a specific rain-provision image beside that reading.

row.basis: Pastures clothed with flocks
row.note: The commentary links its wind-and-cloud aside to the surah’s pasture; Psalm 65 closes with pastures clothed with flocks and valleys covered with grain, a related scene of rain’s result.

row.basis: A nearby neighbor can be closer than distant kin
row.note: The commentary develops the “side” as the place of either companion or stranger and says the reminder remains beside the person; Proverbs values the neighbor who is near over a brother who is far away, giving relational weight to nearness.

row.basis: Wash and make yourselves clean
row.note: The commentary’s triad includes purifying oneself as a deliberate act; Isaiah commands people to wash, make themselves clean, and cease doing evil, a direct ethical image of self-correction.

row.basis: Clean hands and a pure heart
row.note: The commentary says purification is one of the hearer’s own responses; the psalm describes the person fit to approach God as one with clean hands and a pure heart.

row.basis: Make a new heart and turn from transgression
row.note: The commentary links avoiding reminder with a self-made ruin and purification with a chosen response; Ezekiel calls Israel to cast away transgressions and make a new heart and spirit so they may live.

row.basis: Moses asks Pharaoh to humble himself
row.note: The commentary’s Moses asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself, followed by Pharaoh’s rejection; Exodus has Moses and Aaron ask how long Pharaoh will refuse to humble himself before the Lord, making the refusal to heed a direct point of contact.

row.basis: Abraham and Balaam as opposed moral types
row.note: The commentary presents Abraham as entrusting himself to God and seeking distance from idolatry; Avot contrasts disciples of Abraham, marked by humility and a good eye, with Balaam’s pride and acquisitiveness, giving a Jewish ethical interpretation of the Abrahamic posture.

row.basis: Prophetic speech that is heard but not understood
row.note: The commentary stresses one reminder offered while hearers differ in response; Isaiah’s commission says the people will hear without understanding, framing prophetic speech as a judicial hardening, a different emphasis from the commentary’s open invitation.

row.basis: Hearing that does not lead to turning
row.note: The commentary contrasts the person who receives admonition with the one who avoids it; Isaiah’s commission describes closed eyes and dull hearts so the people do not turn and be healed, a contrary account of how the warning functions.

row.basis: The broad road leads to destruction
row.note: The commentary develops two opposed responses and their outcomes; Jesus describes a broad gate and road leading to destruction, entered by many, as a concrete image of the destructive path.

row.basis: The narrow way leads to life
row.note: The commentary contrasts the ashqa with one who receives reminder; Jesus says the narrow way leads to life and is found by few, giving the other side of the two-path image.

row.basis: Hearing or rejecting the messenger
row.note: The commentary says the messenger offers reminder but does not control its reception; Jesus says whoever hears his messengers hears him and whoever rejects them rejects him.

row.basis: Do not refuse the one who speaks
row.note: The commentary ties turning away from reminder to judgment; Hebrews warns its hearers not to refuse the one speaking, recalling that those who rejected the earthly warning did not escape.

row.basis: People will not endure sound teaching
row.note: The commentary says some turn away from reminder because of their chosen response; Paul warns that people will reject sound teaching and gather teachers to suit their desires.

row.basis: Turning the ear from truth
row.note: The commentary makes turning away the decisive act of the ashqa; Paul says people will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths.

row.basis: The Scriptures testify to life
row.note: The commentary says reminder is already present and offered; Jesus says the hearers search the Scriptures, which testify about him.

row.basis: Unwilling to come for life
row.note: The commentary says the wretched one keeps the reminder nearby but will not receive it; Jesus tells his hearers they are unwilling to come to him to have life.

row.basis: People love darkness rather than light
row.note: The commentary describes the person who chooses distance from beneficial reminder; John says people loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil.

row.basis: Evil deeds avoid the light
row.note: The commentary’s avoider moves away from the reminder; John says the one who does evil hates the light and does not come to it, lest his deeds be exposed.

row.basis: Doing truth and coming into the light
row.note: The commentary contrasts turning away with inward moral change; John says the one who does what is true comes to the light so his deeds may be seen as done in God.

row.basis: Love of this life risks losing it
row.note: The commentary links avoiding reminder to preferring the present worldly life; Jesus says the one who loves his life loses it, while the one who hates his life in this world keeps it for eternal life.

row.basis: The rejected stone is precious to believers
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder is differently received; Peter says the stone rejected by builders is precious to those who believe, giving a Christian image of one message/object valued by some and refused by others.

row.basis: A stumbling stone for the disobedient
row.note: The commentary portrays the ashqa as turning aside from what is offered; Peter says others stumble because they disobey the word, a specific outcome of rejection.

row.basis: The word rejected by some hearers
row.note: The commentary says the reminder’s offer is unchanged but its hearers divide; Paul and Barnabas say their hearers have rejected the word and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life.

row.basis: Other hearers rejoice and believe
row.note: The commentary contrasts the person who turns away with the one who receives reminder; Acts says Gentile hearers rejoice and believe after the same proclamation that some rejected.

row.basis: Jesus makes Nineveh’s repentance a witness
row.note: The commentary treats taking warning as the positive alternative to turning away; Jesus says Nineveh repented at Jonah’s proclamation and will condemn the generation that refuses a greater warning, a Christian rereading of Jonah’s response.

row.basis: The crowd silences a blind petitioner
row.note: The commentary recounts a blind man who comes seeking help while another turns away from him; Mark’s crowd rebukes blind Bartimaeus and tells him to be silent, but he cries out all the more.

row.basis: The blind petitioner follows the way
row.note: The commentary pairs the blind man’s humble approach with the person who avoids admonition; Jesus restores Bartimaeus and he follows Jesus on the road, a distinct reversal in which the blind petitioner responds and follows.

row.basis: Invited guests make excuses
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder is offered but its recipients choose whether to respond; in Jesus’ banquet parable, the invited guests begin making excuses and refuse the invitation.

row.basis: The blind and poor are brought to the feast
row.note: The commentary’s Abasa scene gives attention to a blind seeker whom a prominent person neglects; after the invited guests refuse, the servant brings the poor, crippled, blind, and lame to the banquet.

row.basis: The blind see and the seeing are judged
row.note: The commentary uses the blind visitor to expose the failure of a sighted, socially prominent person to recognize who may benefit; Jesus says he came so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind.

row.basis: Claimed sight leaves guilt intact
row.note: The commentary opposes the humble blind seeker to the one who turns away; Jesus tells the Pharisees that their claim to see leaves their sin, unlike the blind man whose encounter leads to sight.

row.basis: A messenger leaves when a household refuses to hear
row.note: The commentary limits the messenger to offering reminder and leaves response with the audience; Jesus tells messengers to leave and shake the dust off when a house or town will not receive or hear them.

row.basis: Pay attention lest one drift away
row.note: The commentary describes the ashqa as moving away from the reminder; Hebrews urges close attention to what has been heard lest hearers drift away from it.

row.basis: Do not quench the Spirit
row.note: The commentary presents refusal as a response that can suppress what is offered; Paul warns the community not to quench the Spirit.

row.basis: Do not despise prophecies
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is offered but may be put aside; Paul tells the community not to despise prophetic utterances, a direct instruction against rejecting admonition.

row.basis: Work out salvation with fear and trembling
row.note: The commentary reads self-purification and receiving reminder as deliberate action, and distinguishes it from the messenger’s work; Paul tells believers to work out their salvation with fear and trembling.

row.basis: God works in the willing hearer
row.note: The commentary says human response remains dependent on God’s willing; Paul immediately says God is at work in believers both to will and to work, adding divine agency to the self-directed effort.

row.basis: Hearing the voice and opening the door
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is beside a person yet may be kept outside; Revelation pictures Christ standing at a door and knocking, with fellowship following if someone hears and opens.

row.basis: The burdened are invited to rest
row.note: The commentary contrasts the easy path prepared for the messenger with the hardship of the one who rejects guidance; Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him for rest.

row.basis: The yoke is easy and the burden light
row.note: The commentary connects wretchedness with hardship opposite the easy path; Jesus describes his yoke as easy and his burden as light, offering a contrasting response to a divine invitation.

row.basis: Torment continues day and night forever
row.note: The commentary reads the condemned condition as prolonged, with neither death nor life; Revelation portrays the devil and the beast’s followers as tormented day and night forever, a related image of unending punishment.
